item.title: Ukraine war briefing: Finland urges Elon Musk to expand Kyiv’s Starlink coverage over Russia
item.description:
Ukraine believes that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target missile launchers. What we know on day 1,675

Finnish President Alexander Stubb has said he pleaded with SpaceX owner Elon Musk to expand Starlink satellite internet coverage for Ukraine so it can strike Russian ballistic missile launchers located inside ⁠Russian territory. Ukraine ⁠has an acute shortage ​of air defences to repel Russian ballistic missiles and Kyiv believes that turning on Starlink over Russian territory would help it target the launchers that fire the missiles. Musk switched on the Starlink satellite internet service over ‌Ukraine shortly after Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022. It has become the lifeblood of Ukraine’s battlefield communications and a tool for piloting drones, but it does not work over Russian territory.

Volodymyr Zelenskyy has met with senior Wall Street executives on ​the sidelines of the UN general assembly in New York, ⁠as Kyiv seeks to attract investments to help finance the country’s rebuilding efforts. The meeting focused mainly ⁠on areas such as helping Ukraine get through the winter and supporting its economy, the Ukrainian ⁠government said. Ukraine faces a brutal winter as stepped-up Russian strikes on ​its infrastructure and key ‌export industries deepen ‌the country’s budget crisis. The daily cost of the war ‌grew to about $190m this year. The meeting, attended by more than two dozen US companies, was facilitated by US banking giant Citigroup and the US chamber of commerce.

Russia could launch a limited military attack against a Nato country in the coming months, Danish intelligence said, in one of the starkest warnings yet by western security services. In a report published on Thursday, the Danish defence intelligence service warned of a “low but growing risk” that Russia could launch long-range strikes on Nato infrastructure supporting Ukraine, or carry out a limited incursion into a neighbouring country with a small number of troops, potentially operating without insignia. The report came hours after a fire at a Starlink satellite station in central Poland that local authorities described as an “act of sabotage”.

Nato is capable of handling sabotage and drone incidents in Europe and has good action plans in place to deal with them, the alliance’s secretary general said after the warning from Danish intelligence. Secretary-general Mark Rutte said he believes the rising number of hybrid incidents in Nato countries shows that Russian President Vladimir Putin is losing the war in Ukraine. He said that citizens of the 32 Nato countries can remain calm. “Putin is in a bad place,” Rutte said. “He is not winning the war in Ukraine.”

Russian drone and missile strikes on Kyiv and Ukraine’s north-east killed eight people on ⁠Thursday in attacks that included ⁠a maternity hospital and a ​farm, officials said. Two people died ⁠in the assault on Kyiv, Zelenskyy said. “As people were sleeping, flashes from explosions lit up the sky,” the president said on Telegram. Police said nine homes, a post office, ​warehouses and dozens of cars were also damaged in Kyiv. A separate ‌Russian attack on a vegetable storage ‌facility at a farm in a village of the north-eastern Kharkiv region killed six people and injured a further 12, prosecutors said.

⁠Turkish president Tayyip Erdogan said Turkey ⁠had ⁠stepped up ​efforts to re-establish the Black ⁠Sea grain corridor. “We have now increased ⁠our efforts to ​re-establish ‌the grain corridor. ‌We are also ‌accelerating our diplomatic steps for this,” Erdogan told a group of Turkish journalists ‌in New York. Erdogan said ⁠he had discussed ​the ​issue again ​with Zelenskyy ‌and received ​a ​positive response.

Copenhaver was in the bleachers during the event in Butler, Pennsylvania, when a 20-year-old gunman opened fire from a nearby rooftop, grazing Trump’s right ear with one bullet. Copenhaver was struck in the arm and in the abdomen, wounds that left him with lingering injuries and walking with a cane.

Navigating a More Uncertain World: Lessons from CIA’s Red Cell
item.description:
Twenty-five years after 9/11, the United States is confronting yet another era of profound uncertainty and potential dangers. The pace and scale of change are creating unforeseen disruptions that impact our security, stability, and prosperity. Advancing technologies are being adopted and applied in unexpected ways, sparking debates about the unintended consequences for human existence. No longer can we sit back and wait to be surprised.

In the wake of 911, the CIA stood up the Red Cell to address a systemic failure of imagination and later reaffirmed this mission after the intelligence failures of the Iraq War. As memories have faded, the appetite for bold, contrarian thinking has waned, but we remain one unforeseen act of violence, one slow-burning and overlooked development, one scientific breakthrough away from the next shock. In this essay, those who served in the Red Cell look back on its history to derive lessons for better navigating this uncertain future. Now is not a time for cautious assessments but fearless exploration. Leaders in the public and private sectors must be ready to navigate a broader range of possible futures. The safety, security, and livelihoods of future generations depend on such forward thinking.

The Origin of the Red Cell

It was September 12, 2001, just 24 hours after the tragic attacks of 9/11. The American people were in shock and struggling to make sense of what had happened. The United States had experienced a strategic surprise as unfathomable as the Pearl Harbor attack in 1941.

At CIA headquarters in Virginia that morning, Director of Central Intelligence George Tenet gathered Deputy Director for Intelligence Jami Miscik and two distinguished analytic managers, Robert Ovelmen and Paul Frandano, to find a way to compel the bureaucracy to go beyond what it knew and what it assessed and to consider what could be. With a simple but bold mandate, “tell me what others don’t” and “make seniors feel uncomfortable,” he commissioned them to create a new analytic unit, called the Red Cell, to challenge conventional wisdom on terrorism. (Foreign Policy) Neither Ovelmen nor Frandano were experts on terrorism or the Middle East, but they were known for their strong analytic skills, exceptional command of history, understanding of policymaker needs, and somewhat quirky personalities. This cell was not limited to traditional Cold War-style “red teaming” that focused on roleplaying the adversary, but instead it was a more expansive effort to explore possibilities.

Tenet gave them great latitude to gather talent from across the intelligence enterprise. While the mission initially was limited to terrorism and the Middle East, the analysts they recruited had worked everything but those issues. Having experienced the unthinkable, these analysts were tasked to stretch their imaginations to consider the full range of plausible next events. The first products were short and pithy, with catchy titles and provocative ideas about the nature of attack and what the coming days and weeks could portend. The first Red Cell analysis was published two days later on 14 September. Tenet took it directly into the Oval Office, and President George W. Bush asked for more.

Within the first year, the Red Cell was tasked to go beyond its original focus on terrorism and branch into other issues. In the run up to the invasion of Iraq in 2003, the Red Cell produced a flurry of products on what Iraqi President Saddam Husayn might do to prevent an attack and how he might react. The presentations and argumentation were deliberately eye-catching and evocative to make readers engage with the ideas and to remember them the next day. Ovelmen and Frandano knew the avalanche of information and meetings senior policymakers faced each day and wanted the ideas to stand out and be considered, even if they were later dismissed.

This strategy was not without controversy. Some ideas were not only bold but contradicted by existing facts. Others unwittingly were uncomfortably close to highly sensitive policies and plans. Some military commanders in the field worried that the Red Cell might give their superiors dangerous ideas. Expert analysts across the IC were often furious, especially if a Red Cell idea created a tasking for them. Sometimes CIA seniors had to remind readers that the Red Cell was not the authoritative assessment. Even with these challenges, the Red Cell continued to have senior-level support. One senior policymaker once said, “tell those analysts I disagree with this but also tell them to keep writing it.” In his 2006 confirmation testimony to become CIA director, General Michael Hayden said, "Red cell alternative analysis and red cell alternative evaluations are a rich source of thought-provoking estimates, and they should be a part, an integral part, of our analysis.” (Senate Select Committee on Intelligence, May 18, 2006)

BOX: Original mission statement: “In response to the events of 11September, the Director of Central Intelligence commissioned CIA ‘s Deputy Director for Intelligence to create a "red cell " that would think unconventionally about the full range of relevant analytic issues. The DCI Red Cell is thus charged with taking a pronounced "out-of-the-box " approach and will periodically produce memoranda and reports intended to provoke thought rather than to provide authoritative assessments.”

The Next Generation – Red Cell 2.0

As the Red Cell approached the end of the decade, the remaining original members planned to retire. They assumed they would be told to turn off the lights and lock the vault. They had a good run! They had many fans and probably an equal number of skeptics. Contrary to their expectations, then–CIA Deputy Director for Analysis Michael Morell tasked them to find a new set of leaders to carry on the work and train the next generation.

However, with greater distance from the tragedy of 9/11, the interest in and tolerance for the most extreme ideas had waned among some audiences. Both policymakers and the intelligence leadership wanted Red Cell products to have more grounding in tradecraft and data while still considering alternative trajectories and expanding thinking on the various possibilities. The new Red Cell leadership recognized the challenge to preserve and maintain the “Redness” while grounding the assessments with rigorous research and data. To meet these competing demands, they launched Red Cell 2.0, refreshing the brand and expanding the style, argumentation, and presentation.

The Red Cell still had top-level support to delve into the thorniest issues. In September 2012, CIA Director David Petraeus reiterated and expanded the mission, telling the Red Cell to “take on our most difficult intelligence challenges” and “shock us.” During this time, both senior military officers and policymakers found value in Red Cell analysis. Lt. General H.R. McMaster recalled that “As National Security Advisor and as a military commander in combat, I found Red Cell papers useful, in part, because they challenged assumptions and were untainted by and often ran counter to policy preferences.”

Other leaders wanted to participate in the brainstormings because Red Cell analysts challenged them. Supreme Allied Commander NATO, Admiral James Stavridis described engaging with the Red Cell team as “an intellectual adventure that forced my senior staff to interrogate our assumptions, consider more extreme futures for the Alliance, and to understand the choices and risks involved in each scenario.” Red Cell engagements often kicked off with a provocative prompt to disarm the participants and to pave the way for a more open and productive conversation. In one such engagement, a Red Cell analyst launched with “sir, if you were indicted for war crimes.” Although taken aback by such an outlandish suggestion, the prompt changed the tenor of the conversation, and this senior leader became a regular consumer of Red Cell analysis.

To add rigor and maintain credibility, the cell directly addressed perceived analytic tradecraft weaknesses, built partnerships with similar units across the US government, systematically interrogated assumptions and biases, and experimented with new ways of conveying analysis. To show their homework, Red Cell analysts sharpened the logic and argumentation of its products and published more point/counterpoint assessments to illuminate both sides of a contentious issue. During this time, CIA leadership reaffirmed the importance of the cell’s mission but encouraged the team to consider scenarios that were smaller deviations from the expected future—rather than being so far out of the box. In response, the Red Cell turned to more multiple scenarios analysis to explore the spectrum of futures from slight variations to more extreme futures. (NPR, May 23, 2012) Some applauded this effort while others complained the Red Cell would lose its edge.

Being a small, experienced, and non-hierarchical unit enabled rapid prototyping. The team experimented with innovative analytic exercises and developed new approaches for delivering complex analytic stories in creative, memorable ways. For example, the team kicked off each year with a highly engaging, day-long exercise called “Ideapalooza” to push beyond the expected future and explore the intersection of trends and dynamics. (Foreign Policy) The Red Cell was the first unit to publish a fully interactive, choose-your-own-adventure, analytic product, enabling analysts and policymakers to test the impact of different variables. The Red Cell experimented with delivering analysis as a graphic novel. To present difficult messages, the Red Cell drew on historical analogies, turns of phrase, and even pop culture. From song references like “Back in the USSR” to puns about the cold when writing about the Arctic to provocative titles like “Anticipating Saddam’s Last Gasp Gambits,” “Saddam’s Eleventh Hour Options,” and “What If the US Is Seen as an Exporter of Terrorism,” the Red Cell pushed the limits to make scenarios vivid and spark the imagination.

While maintaining its creative environment, the Red Cell often tackled some of the most serious and challenging national security questions. The NSC called upon the Red Cell to produce highly speculative, strategic perspectives on global issues that did not lend themselves to more traditional, heavily sourced intelligence products, such as the future of geopolitics, the durability of alliances, and the international order. These products were less challenge analysis and more thought provoking, big picture assessments. The collocation of senior analysts from different disciplines and with experiences working different regions and issues was an advantage in tackling broad, strategic global issues.

Moving from a Cell to a Product Line

In the most significant evolution since the creation of the Red Cell, in 2023 the Red Cell ceased to be a standalone unit and became a product line under the direction of a Red Cell chief. No longer was there a dedicated staff or separate offices. Instead, Red Cells would now be written by the expert analysts, managed and edited by a senior-level analyst in negotiation with regional and issue managers. There are obvious pros and cons to this new approach.

  • On the plus side, products could draw on the expertise of those who know the topic best and can see more nuanced variations. Moreover, when published, the assessments would have high-level support, increasing the possibility of policymakers reading them.
  • However, it is difficult to question your own, well-researched and -reasoned analytic line, especially one that has held up to time and events. During crises, expert analysts rarely have the time to pull away from daily coverage of events to consider alternatives and question assumptions. Human nature is to expect the future to be like the present, and it often requires an outsider who is not burdened by expertise to ask the fundamental questions. For example, in 2011, regional analysts in the early days of the Arab Spring were covering the crisis 24/7 with situation reports and daily assessments. The Red Cell was able to explore provocative questions, such as “is this an end-of-history moment”, and could develop multiple scenarios for how the crisis might end.

Shades of Red

Looking back on this work, Red Cell products have always had many shades of red, ranging from far outside the box—almost crimson analysis—to products that were just a subtle but important deviation from the mainline–pink. Sometimes the situation called for a complete 180-degree contrarian take on how the world could go in the opposite direction, but in other situations the Red Cell looked to stress-test underlying assumptions or pursue multiple scenarios. From the beginning, the Red Cell focused on a few analytic techniques or prompts to help tease out subtleties and other perspectives.

  • A popular and effective approach was What-If analysis. This approach recognized the most likely future trajectory but then asked, what if something changed? These pieces explored both why something different might happen and what the consequences might be.
  • Devil’s Advocacy—a true contrarian alternative—was sometimes but not often the line of argumentation. More frequently, the piece offered a range of ways a situation could evolve or various perspectives a foreign actor might hold.
  • Another favorite but more difficult approach which was used from the beginning was the first-person narrative in which the Red Cell tried to channel the strategies, calculations, and even fears of key leaders like Saddam Husayn and Usama Bin Laden. (CIA Reading Room)
  • An important and analytically rigorous technique was the assumptions check in which the Red Cell would identify and interrogative important underlying assumptions about an issue.
  • Multiple scenarios papers delivered variations of the future from very “red” storylines to trajectories that are largely continuations of the status quo. Some scenarios were mutually exclusive while others offered sequential developments.
  • Team A/B or Point/Counterpoint papers explored opposing explanations or arguments about the future. Sometimes, these were delivered in a debate style.

Assessing the Value of the Red Cell

There are many misconceptions about the role of such a contrarian unit. Many tried to assess the value of Red Cell products based on accuracy, assuming that predicting the future better than the mainline analytic experts was the goal. However, the Red Cell was never designed to be right or to provide authoritative assessments. Judging the value of the Red Cell based on how often its alternative analysis was right misses the point. In fact, the Red Cell should be wrong most of the time, given the exceptional expertise and analysis conducted by the Intelligence Community every day. When the Red Cell was right, the mainline analysis by definition had missed something.

At its core, the mission of the Red Cell was to help US decision-makers prepare for a greater range of possible futures to make our nation safer, stronger, and more resilient in the face of growing uncertainty and to give them decision advantage. The Red Cell achieved this by widening the aperture on any situation and exploring plausible—not necessarily probable—futures. The real value was in making people think, making them curious, provoking debate, and helping them understand the underlying foundations of their assessments. Done right, the Red Cell identified analytic weaknesses and helped make mainline analysis stronger. Helping analytic colleagues strengthen their assessments was more important than delivering a finished product to a senior policymaker.

Here are few ways to consider the value and usefulness:

  • Did decision-makers read it? Yes, some more than others. Many read the analysis even—and especially—if they disagreed with it as a check on their own thinking.
  • Did analysts and warfighters read Red Cells? Absolutely. Red Cell products were among the most read analytic products in the Intelligence Community over multiple years.
  • Did Red Cells spark debate? Almost always. It created discussions, which was the point.
  • Did senior decision-makers ask for Red Cell papers? Quite often.
  • Did Red Cell products influence policy discussions and even choices? Again, yes. In one instance, the NSC reworked a regional strategy in light of a Red Cell memo that foresaw the involvement of a major international player. (Forbes)
  • Did the Red Cell shift and improve the culture of mainline analytic units? Yes. Over time many offices incorporated Red Cell techniques, and some created their own contrarian in-house units. Red Cell alumni often went back to “regular” units, in effect, becoming evangelists for out-of-the-box thinking and analysis.
  • Have others incorporated these techniques and approaches? Yes, in foreign governments, international institutions, and private companies, entities like the Red Cell—some even called the Red Cell—now exist around the world. (Stimson Center) (Red Cell Partners)Georgetown University has created a Master’s Degree that includes Red Cell projects. (Georgetown University) In 2023, the Stimson Center—a Washington-based think tank—created its own unit called the Red Cell which takes “a devil’s advocate approach to US foreign policy” and “puts forward innovative solutions and unorthodox thinking about America’s role in the world.” (Stimson Center)

Secrets of Success

The success of the Red Cell stemmed from the combination of circumstances, design, and leadership. The shock and fear generated by the attacks on 9/11, followed by flawed intelligence assessments of Iraq’s WMD programs, created the environment for more speculative, creative, and provocative analytic assessments. To meet this demand, CIA leadership made several important choices to create a unique unit with the authority to explore, question, challenge, and go beyond the data. Moreover, they let the ideas be heard, even when they were on the edge and even when they disagreed with them. However, over time, as memories of 9/11 faded, the conditions that facilitated and protected bold analysis evaporated or were dismantled one after another.

Top Cover: With a mandate to make leaders uncomfortable, success required absolute assurance and top cover. That top cover came from both senior analytic managers and senior customers and was reiterated often in the early days.

The Process: The Red Cell also was given the freedom to write and publish without going through formal Intelligence Community coordination processes. The Red Cell was required to consult, but not to coordinate. It could—and often did—disagree with the mainline, coordinated point of view. It weighed the evidence differently. It took speculative leaps. In contrast, mainline analysis had to reflect the views and expertise of the entire organization; every analytic unit with a stake in the topic got to weigh in, and the originating office was obligated to take these views on board. Judgments had to be rigorously supported with multiple citations and sources. This process is what made the end result an CIA product, not an individual one. It ensured that all the evidence is considered and all defensible points of view are reflected. A great deal of time and effort went into coordination, and it was a point of pride for analysts to do it well and come up with an agreed analytic line.

Talent and Staffing: Being a member of and writing for the Red Cell required insatiable curiosity, a willingness to ask tough questions and go against the grain, and a propensity to see angles others didn’t. Red Cell analysts had to be fearless and willing to speak truth to power no matter the consequences. To find such talent, CIA leaders gave the Red Cell authority to recruit from across the organization and request officers from other agencies, including those senior analysts who had topped out and thus, had little fear of pushing analytic boundaries. The cell combined a few core, long-term members with frequent rotations, including from other agencies, to bring fresh ideas and new energy.

Location: Having a designated team outside of the organizational chart and physically separate from expert teams was a key component of the cell’s success. Experts can be too close to a topic or an analytic line to question it. The Red Cell could step back and see a broader landscape of possibilities.

Culture: The Red Cell was about ideas above all else and promoted a culture of exploration, play, and divergent thinking. Rank was left at the door–even for senior military officers. The work always started with conversation/brainstorming—not an unusual method—but in the cell brainstorming sessions preceded every analytic effort. The art of the conversation is teasing out ideas first. Collaboration was another critical component; Red Cell analysts often co-authored products or developed projects with other offices, agencies, governments, academia, and the private sector. No one has a monopoly on innovation or good ideas.

Conveying Analysis: Creativity in argumentation and presentation brought the unlikely future scenarios to life for skeptical consumers. The Red Cell experimented with new formats, visual aids, and graphics, and it worked closely with designers, cartographers and videographers.

Lessons for an Uncertain Future

Twenty-five years since the establishment of the Red Cell, the future environment appears even more uncertain, more prone to unprecedented disruptions, and potentially more dangerous. The combination of rapidly advancing technologies, hyper connectivity, changing international norms and institutions, discontented publics, and the return of great-power competition has created a world in flux. Change is happening at a breathtaking pace and scale with implications for our security, stability, and prosperity. Dynamics that were unimaginable even five years ago are now reality.

Experience continues to show the high probability of being surprised by low-probability events. Organizations of all types remain vulnerable to groupthink, confirmation bias, and assuming the future will be like the present. Such well-known organizational and human behaviors lie at the root of historical policy and intelligence failures. Red Cell-type organizations help guard against these tendencies and compel consideration of alternatives.

To anticipate, manage, and thrive in these divergent futures, now is the time for more Red Cell-like thinking in every sector—both public and private. Leaders and decision-makers must be ready to navigate a broader range of possible futures, including inevitable strategic surprises. Now is not a time for cautious assessments but fearless exploration. The safety, security, and livelihoods of future generations depend on such forward thinking.

Drawing on our years of analytic experience and thinking the unthinkable, this group of Red Cell alumni offers several suggestions to improve future readiness for our communities, our industries, and our country.

  • Institutionalize a challenge function: Create a dedicated effort with a broad mandate and direct, unfettered access to the top leadership (CEOs, directors, commanders, etc.) Such a team should be charged with challenging assumptions, questioning longstanding practices, and exploring low probability-high impact scenarios.
  • Explore a broader range of futures: Stress-test goals and policies across a range of plausible futures to improve resilience, increase flexibility, and take advantage of emerging opportunities.
  • Think multidisciplinary and interdisciplinary: Dynamics and trends can no longer be analyzed in isolation. The world is too complex and connected.
  • Go beyond the obvious: It is in the second- and third-order implications where surprises tend to occur, often from seemingly small development that cascade over time.
  • Give permission to fail: Instill a ”start-up” mindset, where many investments are dead-ends but a few pay off in a big way.
  • Be FEARLESS. The world is depending on you.

item.title: Denmark’s Greenland deal with Trump is a victory for diplomacy over bullying
item.description:
Denmark’s Greenland deal with Trump is a victory for diplomacy over bullying Expert comment jon.wallace 24 September 2026

Denmark used its soft power to rally support and took the dispute out of the limelight – addressing underlying US interests instead of President Trump’s unacceptable public position.

This week, Denmark has extricated itself from a period of coercive US diplomacy over Greenland. The agreement announced on 22 September elegantly resolves the dispute over the territory, without forcing Denmark or the government of Greenland to give up very much. 

Even before the dispute, Denmark had indicated it would be content to increase the number of US bases in Greenland and enhance US access to them. These measures were already possible under an existing 1951 agreement. 

The new agreement adds an undertaking by Denmark and Greenland to refuse major investments from non-members of the EU or NATO that would grant them a foothold in strategic Arctic areas. Again, on this point, Washington was pushing on an open door.

The only meaningful change concerns the mechanism to ensure that this arrangement will be permanent. The 1951 agreement, amended in 2004, also does not expire. But the new text adds that Greenland will remain part of NATO and continue to comply with the agreement, should it opt for independence. 

An independent Greenland might have been willing to retain the US bases and related agreements anyway. After all, it would need to rely on US defence support and a NATO security guarantee. But expressly making these points in an agreement co-signed by Greenland overcame the deal-breaker of President Donald Trump’s demand for sovereignty over all of Greenland or at least the US base areas.

The agreement represents a masterclass by Denmark in using the classical art of diplomacy to overcome bullying, in an age of changing geopolitics and unstable global governance. 

Indeed, the steps Denmark took to resolve the dispute provide valuable insight into how countries can defend their interests in the face of apparently overwhelming pressure.

Step 1: Isolate the bully and call the game

In January this year, President Trump declared that the US would need to ‘own’ Greenland to prevent Russia or China from taking it, and to ensure US national security. He even raised the option of a military takeover of the territory.

The president may have believed opposition would be minimal. Just days before, EU and NATO countries had been unwilling to confront him publicly over the armed US intervention against Venezuela, despite it being a clear breach of international law. In the emergency meeting of the UN Security Council that followed, they had stayed meekly silent. 

Greenland was different. Denmark could clearly assert that Trump was placing the future of NATO in peril. Hence, Denmark could show that the US action posed a threat to both the territorial integrity of Denmark and to the security of all states in Western Europe. Accordingly, NATO countries and EU members overcame their hesitancy to upset the White House, and strongly and unanimously rejected his demand. Indeed, they went further, dispatching a European defence mission to Greenland, supposedly as a matter of routine.

Calling out the US’s game for what it was – a demand to surrender national territory under the threat of force at a time when the West was resisting Putin’s assault on Ukraine – was crucial in rallying support.

Step 2: Enter the fray with clean hands

In this dispute, Denmark continually had the advantage in the battle for international sympathy. It entered the fray with clean hands, taking advantage of its soft power, which has been nurtured over decades of sensitive advocacy for justice in relation to the Global South and the international rule of law. The US under Trump, on the other hand, has caused continued upset throughout, as a result of its military actions and other activity such as the president’s sweeping ‘Liberation Day’ tariffs.

The US could also not accuse Denmark of hypocrisy over any supposed colonial legacy relating to Greenland. By 1954, the UN General Assembly had determined that Greenland had freely decided to integrate with Denmark on the basis of equal constitutional and administrative standing with other parts of Denmark. 

By 1979 Copenhagen offered home rule. Two decades later, in 2009, it granted wide-ranging self-government to Greenland. Crucially, this 2009 arrangement included an express right of self-determination for the people of Greenland, with a provision to opt for independence. Any sale of Greenland (as Trump had previously proposed) or its transfer to the US against the wishes of the population, would have violated this existing right to self-determination. 

This meant that throughout the dispute, Denmark could claim a role as both the upholder of the international right to self-determination, and the defender of its own territorial integrity.

Step 3: Clarify the legal status

President Trump sought to enhance his claim by suggesting that Denmark did not have a clear title to Greenland. In view of the 2009 agreement’s self-determination provisions, this assertion became less relevant. In any event, it was easy to prove that Denmark held good title. And the US clearly had none at all. 

In 1916 US Secretary of State Robert Lansing issued a declaration accepting Denmark’s claim to the island. When the US took over the defence of Greenland during Germany’s occupation of Denmark during the Second World War, it did so in ‘recognition and respect for the sovereignty of the Kingdom of Denmark over Greenland.’ 

This expressly included Danish sovereignty over base areas constructed by the US. The post-war agreements on defence cooperation and US bases of 1951 and 2004 also consistently confirmed Danish sovereignty. Indeed, in an amazing reversal of the US position, so does the new 2026 agreement. The text reaffirms the sovereignty and territorial integrity of Denmark and acknowledges Greenland’s right to self-determination. 

Step 4: Dial the temperature down and let experts do the work

When encountering the US, Denmark was careful to avoid a public confrontation with Trump in front of cameras, learning from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s experience at the Oval Office in 2025. 

Instead, when the row intensified, Copenhagen dispatched Foreign Minister Lars Lokke Rasmussen to Washington. As foreign minister, protocol demanded that he should meet with the slightly more moderate US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, instead of the president. 

Vice President JD Vance almost derailed this cunning plan when he insisted on leading the meeting and moving it to the White House. But Rasmussen, a former Danish prime minister, calmly focused on shared security interests in the Arctic. And he remained steadfast where sovereignty and the rights of Greenlanders were concerned.

After a supposed breakthrough on the issue at the Davos conference later in January 2026, Denmark managed to divert dialogue to technical meetings, held confidentially, outside of the public eye. This was the critical change that allowed Copenhagen to defang the entire episode.

Step 5: Focus on interests, not positions

Negotiations experts know that success depends on persuading the sides to step away from their incompatible, publicly stated position and instead address their underlying interests. In this instance, President Trump had claimed that only full sovereignty over Greenland would answer US security needs. 

At Davos, NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte offered the US sovereignty at least over its base areas in Greenland. Trump seized that initiative and accepted, withdrawing his threat of invasion. 

However, neither Denmark nor Greenland representatives had been party to that proposal. Handing over even a part of sovereign territory would hardly be acceptable to their parliaments.

But in the technical discussions, it became possible to move from a flat-out demand for sovereignty, to achieving the underlying US desire: a permanent arrangement safeguarding its interests in Greenland. 

Step 6: Be generous in victory

On signing the agreement, Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen was careful to avoid any sense of climb-down by President Trump. It is a deal that can ‘last forever,’ she said, reflecting Trump’s claim that he had achieved an outcome just as permanent as a transfer of sovereignty.

As President Trump’s original stated position was that ‘the ownership and control of Greenland is an absolute necessity’, this new agreement seems a clear victory for calm and quiet Danish diplomacy. And it plainly illustrates the power of unity among NATO states and EU members. The lessons for future dealings with great powers are clear.

item.title: Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy
item.description:
Who gets to be Italian? The rise and rise of Islamophobia in Italy

Submitted by Dalia Ismail on Fri, 09/25/2026 - 13:30
Giorgia Meloni's announcement of a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools comes as the Italian right competes over the demonisation of Muslims
A Muslim takes part in a mass in Santa Maria in Trastevere church in Rome on 31 July 2016 (AFP)
Off

When Giorgia Meloni addressed hundreds of young supporters of her Brothers of Italy party in Rome on Sunday, she chose the school as a way of illustrating who she thought was and was not Italian. 

“It cannot be that, in an Italian classroom, Italian children are the ones who feel cornered because they have become the minority. It cannot happen,” the prime minister told Fenix, the annual festival organised by National Youth, Brothers of Italy’s youth wing. 

On Wednesday, Meloni’s government approved a ban on the burqa and niqab in schools and announced that a 30 percent cap will be imposed on children without Italian citizenship or poor knowledge of the Italian language in the first year of primary, middle and high school. 

Meloni described the measures as “common-sense tools that do not divide but really help to integrate”.

The announcement comes as Italy moves towards an expected national election in 2027, with immigration, Islam and national identity once again central battlegrounds on the political right.

Meloni’s speech and the legislation immediately raised practical questions: who exactly is “foreign” and who is Italian? 

Italy already has guidelines recommending a 30 percent ceiling for pupils without Italian citizenship. The distinction between “Italian” and “foreign” children also rests on citizenship, rather than on where children were born or have grown up. 

Italy's citizenship system is based primarily on descent: children born in the country to non-Italian parents generally do not acquire Italian citizenship automatically. 

As a result, children who were born in Italy and have spent their lives there can still be officially classified as foreign citizens. And Meloni's intervention did not come in isolation.

A mosque in Mestre

Last week, a banner declaring “Your integration is our ruin” appeared outside a school in Mestre, on the mainland opposite Venice, in an area with a large Bangladeshi community. Nearby, at a public park used by Muslims for Friday prayers, “No Islam” and Christian crosses were painted on the ground and on a wooden structure.

The incidents come as a dispute over plans by members of Mestre's Bangladeshi community to build a permanent mosque and Islamic centre on the site of a former sawmill becomes increasingly heated. The community has bought the land, but the project requires approval from local authorities.

'We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes'

- Roberto Vannacci, Futuro Nazionale

One of the project's most vocal opponents has been Anna Maria Cisint, a European parliament member for the right-wing Lega party who has repeatedly campaigned against the construction of new mosques. 

In February, during a Lega protest outside the proposed site in Mestre, Cisint declared that the mosque would not be built if her political camp remained in power.

On the same Sunday that Meloni announced her school measures, Cisint appeared at the Lega’s annual rally in Pontida, the northern Italian town that has hosted the party's symbolic gathering for decades. 

She was joined on stage by four activists from Nemesis, a French far-right group that describes itself as feminist. The activists were wearing full-face veils. As people on stage and in the crowd chanted “take it off”, the women removed them.

“The threat is radical Islam,” Cisint told the rally. “We will never allow them to Islamise our home. Never.”

The convergence was striking. In Rome, Meloni warned that Italian children could become a minority in classrooms; at Pontida, a coalition politician warned of the country’s “Islamisation”; and in Mestre, a mosque dispute was enflamed by anti-Muslim slogans.

The rogue general

At the same time, another political force is trying to carve out space further to the right.

Roberto Vannacci, a former army general who first became a national figure after publishing a book attacking immigration, feminism and LGBTQ+ rights, entered the European Parliament in 2024 with the Lega. 

The “rogue general” later broke with the party and founded Futuro Nazionale, a new far-right movement that has made “remigration” - the removal of migrants from Italy - one of its defining themes. 

The party is now registering around eight percent in some opinion polls ahead of the next general election, while the Lega, still led by Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini, has fallen below six percent. The figures have intensified a struggle over voters on the Italian right and over how far its politics on immigration and national identity can move.

It was against this backdrop that Vannacci made one of his most explicit statements yet about who should be allowed to become Italian. Speaking at a conference on urban security organised by a police union in Turin on 18 September, he argued that Italy should not make citizenship easier for immigrants.

“We cannot allow an immigrant to become an Italian citizen so easily because then this citizen votes,” Vannacci said. “And when he votes, he does not vote for the good of Italian citizens but for his own good.”

When challenged over whether he was simply worried that naturalised citizens would not vote for him, Vannacci replied: “I'm not afraid that they won't vote for me. I'm afraid that they won't vote for Italy.”

Who gets to be Italian?

The former general’s argument raises a fundamental question: what happens when the person born or raised in Italy actually becomes Italian. 

Fioralba Duma, an Italian-Albanian activist with the campaign group Italians Without Citizenship, told Middle East Eye that Meloni's remarks were particularly troubling because many of the children described as “foreign” have never known another country.

“It is sad, because you realise how little responsibility those in power take when dealing with such important issues, and how little they do to protect children and guarantee them equal opportunities,” she said.

'Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school'

- Ahmed Vall, Islamic Community of Rome

“Our struggle started 10 years ago - and for many people even earlier - but instead of reducing the number of people who are foreigners only on paper, that number continues to grow every year. We used to talk about newly arrived migrants. Today we are talking about third generations: the grandchildren of immigrants, born in Italy.”

Duma’s comments point to a contradiction that has become increasingly visible in Italy's political debate. 

Politicians can speak of “foreign pupils” in classrooms even when those pupils were born in Italy, have spent their lives in the Italian education system and may speak Italian as their first language.

Italy's citizenship law remains largely based on jus sanguinis, or citizenship by descent. A referendum in June 2025 sought to reduce from 10 to five years the period of legal residence required for non-EU adults to apply for citizenship. 

Around two-thirds of those who voted backed the proposal, but turnout was only around 30 percent, well below the 50 percent required for the result to be valid.

The Muslim threat narrative 

The controversy over the proposed mosque in Mestre shows how these arguments are playing out beyond the classroom.

Part of the city's large Bangladeshi community wants to turn the site of the former sawmill into a permanent Islamic centre capable of hosting up to 1,500 worshippers. But the project requires a change in the area's planning designation, and Venice's centre-right mayor, Simone Venturini, has opposed the project.

‘Our land is not for sale’: Italian activists challenge Israeli-linked solar projects
Read More »

Muslim organisations, meanwhile, accuse politicians of turning Islam into a political threat by focusing on issues that have little bearing on the everyday reality of Muslims in Italy.

Ahmed Vall, president of the Islamic Community of Rome, described Meloni's announcement on the niqab as “propaganda”. “We have never seen girls going to school wearing the niqab. It is a false problem,” he told MEE.

“Petrol is approaching three euros a litre, and she is talking about girls wearing the niqab at school when there are no girls wearing the niqab at school,” he said.

Vall said his organisation was prepared to challenge discriminatory measures through legal means, pointing to a complaint already filed against Lega MEP Silvia Sardone after she filmed and confronted a woman wearing a niqab in Turin. 

Rula Mohamed, another Islamic Community of Rome activist, described the situation more starkly, telling MEE that Islamophobia in Italy had reached “extreme levels”.

“What we are seeing today is the extreme result of something that has been cultivated for years,” she said. This climate, Mohamed argued, had been built not just by the right wing, but through years of Muslims being portrayed in the media as dangerous and incompatible with Italian society.

This, she said, had been compounded by the failure of much of the centre-left to seriously confront Islamophobia.

item.title: Pakistan look forward to ‘big test’ as Thailand loom in FIFA Asean Cup opener
item.description:
Pakistan will begin their campaign in the inaugural FIFA ASEAN Cup against a vastly higher-ranked Thailand on Saturday, with head coach Nolberto Solano describing the tournament as an opportunity for his side to measure themselves against some of Asia’s stronger teams.

The Group B Division One opener will kick off at 4:00pm local time (2:00pm PST) at the Si Jalak Harupat Stadium, with Pakistan then scheduled to face the Philippines on Sept 29 and Vietnam on Oct 2.

“We want to use this opportunity to test ourselves against teams like Thailand, Philippines and Vietnam,” Solano said at the pre-match press conference on Friday. “It’s an honour to be here and we know it will be a tough competition.”

The challenge facing Pakistan is reflected in the FIFA rankings. Thailand are currently 94th, while Pakistan are 198th in the latest official rankings.

The Philippines are 135th and Vietnam 113th.

“All our opponents will be very tough and they have fantastic players,” Solano said. “Asian football has been getting better and better so it is a big test for us.

“We are slowly growing, we try to go step by step. We will try to prove ourselves as a national team and see how far we can go in this competition.”

For Pakistan, the tournament comes after an encouraging summer in which Solano’s side won the Diamond Jubilee International Football Tournament in the Maldives.

Pakistan went unbeaten in the four-team event, drawing 0-0 with Bangladesh before beating the Maldives 3-0 and Afghanistan 2-0 in the round-robin stage. They defeated Afghanistan by the same score in the final, with Shayek Dost and Harun Hamid scoring, to secure their first standalone international tournament title in decades.

The triumph also ended a long wait for Pakistan to reach and win a standalone tournament. Their previous final appearance had come at the 1962 Merdeka Cup, while their last tournament triumph before the Maldives success had been a shared title at the Asian Quadrangular Football Tournament in 1952.

The ASEAN Cup, however, presents a markedly different proposition.

Thailand have named a squad featuring veteran playmaker Chanathip Songkrasin, Japan-based midfielder Supachok Sarachat and English-born forward Jude Soonsup-Bell. German-based defender Nicholas Mickelson is also in the squad, under English coach Anthony Hudson.

Thailand’s squad also includes established domestic names such as Supachai Chaided of Buriram United and Peeradon Chamratsamee of Port FC, underlining the depth available to the side.

Pakistan, meanwhile, have assembled a 23-man squad that combines domestic players with a number of footballers based abroad. Captain Abdullah Iqbal will lead the side, while experienced forward Kaleemullah has returned to the national setup.

Defender Easah Suliman, who plays abroad, joined the squad in Bandung after his arrival was delayed by illness. Twenty-two members of the squad had assembled in Indonesia by Thursday, with Easah expected to link up on Friday.

The Pakistan side also includes teenage midfielder Abdul Samad, captain of the national Under-17 team, who recently signed a two-year contract with Azerbaijani champions Qarabag.

For captain Abdullah, the tournament represents a chance for the players to test themselves against opposition of a different calibre.

“It is a great opportunity for us to compete against teams at another level,” he said. “We will try to give our best.”

The FIFA ASEAN Cup is the first edition of a new FIFA tournament involving 14 teams — all 11 ASEAN members plus Bangladesh, Pakistan and Hong Kong China as guest participants. Division One, being staged in Indonesia, comprises eight teams divided into two groups, with the group winners advancing to the final and the runners-up playing for third place.

Pakistan are in the same group as three teams with considerably stronger recent records in Asian football. After Thailand, they face the Philippines on Sept 29 before meeting Vietnam on Oct 2, with all three group matches being played in Bandung except Pakistan’s final fixture against Vietnam, which is scheduled for Jakarta.

For Solano, the immediate objective is less about the size of the challenge and more about how his players respond to it.

“We are slowly growing,” the former Peru international said. “We try to go step by step. We will try to prove ourselves as a national team and see how far we can go in this competition.”

item.title: PM Tarique puts ‘Bangladesh First’ vision before world
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman has used his maiden address to the United Nations General Assembly to present a post-transition vision of Bangladesh built around political and economic empowerment, seeking international partnership to turn the country into a manufacturing hub while declaring: “Bangladesh First: Bangladesh for All.”
Addressing the 81st UN General Assembly in Bangla in New York on Thursday, Tarique laid out what he called a “3-R” strategy -- Recovery, Restoration and Reconstruction -- for rebuilding the country following the political upheaval of 2024.
The 21-minute address, delivered early Friday Bangladesh time, ranged from Bangladesh’s democratic transition and economic ambitions to the Rohingya crisis, climate change, Palestine, artificial intelligence, migration and global conflicts.
“A state cannot become strong while keeping its citizens disempowered,” Tarique said, pledging to build a prosperous, self-reliant and democratic welfare state where people could live with equal rights and dignity regardless of political affiliation, religion or ethnicity.
In one of the central economic messages of the speech, the prime minister said Bangladesh wanted to capitalise on its demographic dividend by transforming its working-age population into skilled human resources, creating large-scale employment and developing the country into a “manufacturing hub”.
He invited development partners to join that effort and said $50 million had been allocated in the current fiscal year to support start-ups led by young entrepreneurs, researchers and innovators.
Tarique also told the international community that Bangladesh welcomed partnerships, innovation and domestic and foreign investment as the government sought to create what he described as a safe, stable and business-friendly country.
On the Rohingya crisis, the prime minister delivered an unequivocal message: the crisis originated in Myanmar and its solution must also be found there.
“The only solution to this problem is the safe repatriation of the displaced Rohingya population to their homeland, Myanmar,” he said, noting that Bangladesh has sheltered more than 1.2 million Rohingyas for over nine years.
He called for firm international support for a lasting solution and urged continued life-saving assistance until repatriation, warning that failure to ensure justice for the displaced population could lead to another humanitarian crisis.
The prime minister also brought Bangladesh’s domestic political transition before the global forum. He described the previous 15 years as a period of “fascist rule and exploitation” and said Bangladesh was now returning to democracy following the 2024 mass uprising and the February 12 national election.
Those characterisations reflected the government’s political account of the transition presented in the speech.
Tarique said his government wanted not only electoral democracy but also the “democratisation of the economy”, so that economic growth reached every family and citizen.
He highlighted Family Cards, Farmers’ Cards, Sports Cards and e-Health Cards, and announced plans to consolidate different assistance programmes under a “Universal Card”.
The Family Card, issued in the name of the female head of a household, was presented as part of the government’s approach to women’s economic empowerment.
Education also featured prominently.
Tarique said the government planned to gradually raise education spending to 5% of GDP over five years, with greater emphasis on technical, practical and employment-oriented education.
On climate change, he sought stronger global action on climate justice, finance and adaptation, while highlighting plans to plant 250 million trees, excavate 20,000 kilometres of canals and advance the Teesta Master Plan and Padma Barrage project.
The prime minister also warned against a new global inequality emerging around artificial intelligence.
“We do not want the digital divide of today to evolve into an artificial intelligence divide in the future,” he said, calling for technology transfer, capacity building and affordable access to modern technology for developing countries.
He urged the UN to develop an effective framework to ensure AI and social media advances were used positively.
On international conflicts, Tarique said dialogue, diplomacy and cooperation should replace military solutions, while reiterating Bangladesh’s support for disarmament and an independent Palestinian state.
With Bangladesh approaching graduation from least-developed-country status, he also called for continued financing, greater market access, technology transfer and capacity-building support to make the transition sustainable.
Tarique closed by setting out the broader political message he wanted to attach to Bangladesh’s next phase: a country where young people could pursue their ambitions without fear, women could live with confidence and every child could have the opportunity to realise their potential.
“That is why we say, ‘Bangladesh First: Bangladesh for All’,” he said.

item.title: Bangladesh reaffirms support for independent, sovereign State of Palestine
item.description:
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam has reiterated Bangladesh’s call for an independent, sovereign and viable State of Palestine on pre-1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, and for Palestine’s full membership in the United Nations.
Shama Obaed attended the High-Level Ministerial Meeting of the Global Alliance for the Implementation of the Two State Solution, held at the UN Headquarters in New York on the sidelines of the 81st session of the UN General Assembly on September 24.
State Minister Shama Obaed called for accelerated implementation of UNSCR 2803 arrangements with clear accountability and Palestinian ownership, protection of UNRWA’s mandate and sustained funding, prevention of forced displacement and demographic change in Gaza and an end to settlement expansion.
The meeting was attended by Ministers and senior representatives from Member States and international organizations, who discussed concrete steps to advance the implementation of the two-state solution.

Cox’s Bazar airport new terminal set to open next week
item.description:
The newly built terminal at Cox’s Bazar airport will open for domestic passenger operations next week, ahead of planned international operations in October, marking a major step towards turning the tourism gateway into an international airport.
“From next week, the new terminal will be used for both arrivals and departures of domestic passengers,” Civil Aviation Authority of Bangladesh (CAAB) Chairman Air Vice Marshal Md Mostafa Mahmood Siddiq said.
The CAAB chairman, who made a final preparatory visit to Cox’s Bazar on Wednesday, said all domestic airlines operating at the airport had made the necessary preparations to shift their passenger-handling activities to the new terminal.
Airlines will initially use golf carts to transport passengers between aircraft and the terminal building, he added.
“After starting domestic operations, we will inaugurate international operations next month from this airport,” Siddiq said.
Director of Marketing and Sales at NOVOAIR Sohail Majid said the airline had completed all preparations and successfully conducted a test run to operate from the new terminal for its passengers.
“We have made all the necessary preparations, including deploying golf carts to use the new terminal,” he said.
The government is preparing to formally inaugurate Cox’s Bazar as an international airport in October following massive investment in upgrading the facility, including the construction of the new terminal and extension of the runway into the Bay of Bengal.
Civil Aviation and Tourism Minister M Rashiduzzaman Millat earlier expressed optimism that Biman Bangladesh Airlines, as well as foreign carriers, would eventually operate international flights from the beach city.
CAAB Member (Operations and Planning) Air Commodore Abu Sayeed Mehboob Khan said, the terminal arrangement would switch to a hybrid system once international operations begin.
Under the planned arrangement, both arriving and departing international passengers will use the new terminal.
Domestic arriving passengers will then use the existing terminal, while departing domestic passengers will complete check-in formalities at the new terminal before proceeding to the old terminal to wait for boarding.
The new terminal forms part of a broader program being implemented by CAAB under the Ministry of Civil Aviation and Tourism to upgrade Cox’s Bazar airport to international standards and make it capable of handling wide-body aircraft.
Currently one of Bangladesh’s busiest domestic airports, Cox’s Bazar handles an average of 28 to 30 passenger aircraft take-offs and landings daily.
CAAB has implemented two development projects and one technical project at the airport to expand its capacity and facilitate direct connectivity between the country’s premier tourism destination and international markets.
The international passenger terminal, covering around 17,956 square meters, has been constructed under a project with an approved cost of approximately Tk 362.63 crore.
The terminal includes a departure lounge capable of accommodating 450 international passengers, a duty-free shop, boarding bridge, lifts, escalators, conveyor belts, check-in desks, departure and arrival immigration counters and an arrival lounge.
Four immigration desks have been installed for departing passengers and six for arriving passengers, while two baggage delivery belts have been provided for international arrivals.
PA and Flight Information Display Systems (FIDS), signage, CCTV and heavy hand-luggage scanning facilities have also been incorporated into the terminal.
The airport’s annual passenger handling capacity is expected to rise from around 730,000 to 1.8 million following the expansion.
A 36,300-square-metre apron capable of accommodating two wide-body aircraft and three Dash-8 aircraft, along with two taxiways, has already been completed and incorporated into airport operations.
Parking facilities for 35 VIP and 90 general vehicles, internal roads and other supporting infrastructure are also included in the project.
The airport has also received ICAO certification following verification of the standards required for international operations.
Another major component of the transformation is the extension of the runway from 9,000 feet to 10,700 feet, making it the longest runway in Bangladesh.
Around 43 hectares of land have been reclaimed from the Bay of Bengal to extend the runway by 1,700 feet.
The extended runway is designed to accommodate fully loaded wide-body aircraft, including Boeing 777-300ER and Boeing 747-400 aircraft.
The runway extension project has an approved cost of Tk 3,709.61 crore, while the contract value is Tk 1,794.31 crore. Chinese joint venture CYWEB-CCECC JV has implemented the project.
The project also includes around 2,200 feet of precision approach lighting extending into the sea and installation of a CAT-II Airfield Ground Lighting system to facilitate safe aircraft operations.
A 1.89-kilometre protective embankment has been constructed to protect the runway from cyclones, storm surges and other natural disasters, while security fencing, patrol roads and an 8,149-metre drainage system are also part of the project.
The government expects direct international air connectivity to help attract more foreign tourists and stimulate investment in hotels, resorts and other tourism-related businesses in Cox’s Bazar.

Bangladesh, Trinidad and Tobago sign MoU on bilateral consultations
item.description:
Bangladesh and Trinidad and Tobago have signed a memorandum of understanding (MoU) to establish regular bilateral consultations, with Bangladesh identifying energy cooperation as a priority for early discussions.
State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir and Trinidad and Tobago's Minister of Foreign and CARICOM Affairs SM Sobers signed the MoU in New York on Thursday, according to a press release received on Friday.
Kobir said the mechanism would allow the two countries to review their relations regularly, pursue commercial, economic, scientific, technical and cultural cooperation, and exchange views on regional and international issues.
He called energy one of the most promising areas for near-term cooperation and sought Sobers' support for an early technical meeting between relevant organizations from the two countries.
The Trinidad and Tobago participants could include the National Gas Company, Atlantic LNG, Phoenix Park Gas Processors and an ammonia or fertilizer producer, the release said.
Kobir also sought Trinidad and Tobago's support for sustained international attention to the Rohingya crisis, including during its 2027-2028 term on the UN Security Council. Bangladesh continues to shelter more than 1.2 million Rohingyas from Myanmar, he said, amid declining humanitarian funding.
He called for their safe, voluntary, dignified and sustainable return to Myanmar.
Describing cricket as a link between the two countries, Kobir proposed exchanges in youth and women's cricket, coaching, sports science and sports administration.
Both sides expressed hope that the MoU would make their longstanding friendly relationship more structured and substantive.

item.title: PM outlines 3-R strategy at UNGA to rebuild Bangladesh
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Thursday told the international community that Bangladesh was pursuing a three-R strategy — Recovery, Restoration and Reconstruction — to rebuild the country after more than a decade-and-a-half of what he described as fascist rule and exploitation.
Addressing the general debate of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly at UN Headquarters in New York, he also called for resolving global conflicts through dialogue and diplomacy, while urging stronger international action on the Rohingya crisis, climate change, disarmament, migration and equitable access to technology.
“Bangladesh became free from fascism in 2024, bringing an end to more than one and a half decades of fascist rule and exploitation. Having freed itself from the scourges of enforced disappearances and killings, abductions, corruption, looting and money laundering that had become the norm under fascist rule, Bangladesh is now once again embarking on the path of democracy,” Tarique said.
He said an immense horizon of possibilities was now open before Bangladesh and the government had begun implementing extensive programmes to transform the country’s working-age population into skilled human resources by taking advantage of the demographic dividend.
Tarique said Bangladesh also wanted to develop as a “manufacturing hub” and sought support from development partners in this endeavour.
The government, he said, had allocated US$50 million in the current fiscal year to create opportunities for young entrepreneurs, researchers and innovators to implement start-up initiatives.
“Detailed measures have been taken to create extensive employment opportunities and develop Bangladesh as a ‘manufacturing hub’,” he said, seeking support from Bangladesh’s development partners in this endeavour.
The Prime Minister said more than half of Bangladesh’s population were women. and women were therefore at the forefront of all government plans for the country’s socio-economic transformation.
The government was giving priority to women’s education, employment and entrepreneurship, he said, adding that opportunities for cash financing for women, particularly in the small and medium-sized industries sector, had been expanded to support the creation of women entrepreneurs.
Tarique also said opportunities for free education for women up to the undergraduate level had been made available.
He said the government wanted to ensure not only electoral democracy but also the ‘democratisation of the economy’ so that the benefits of economic growth and prosperity reached every family and citizen.
To achieve this, the government had introduced support programmes for economically disadvantaged people through various social protection schemes, including the Family Card, Farmers’ Card, Sports Card and e-Health Card, he said.
“The government considers the ‘Family Card’, issued in the name of the female head of each household, to be a symbol of women’s economic empowerment,” Tarique said.
He said the government also planned to introduce a ‘Universal Card’ by integrating the cards introduced to provide support in every sector.
This was Tarique Rahman’s maiden address to the UN General Assembly. He delivered the speech in Bangla, as announced earlier by his office.
Standing on the same platform where his father, Shaheed President Ziaur Rahman, and mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, had addressed the world, Tarique said he was speaking for the interests of Bangladesh and its people and with the hope of a peaceful world community.
Paying tribute to the martyrs of Bangladesh’s Liberation War, he also recalled those killed and injured during the July-August 2024 mass uprising early on in his speech.
He said after a prolonged period of fighting fascism, Bangladesh had entrusted the Bangladesh Nationalist Party with the responsibility of governing the country through the February 12 national election, describing the people as the source of all political power.
The Prime Minister said human-made conflicts had created unrest, displacement and humanitarian crises in many parts of the world, while wars and conflicts were putting severe pressure on the global economy, energy security and inflation.
“We believe that any conflict should be resolved through dialogue, diplomatic processes and mutual cooperation,” he said.
He said equality, fairness, protection of mutual interests, respect and dignity should form the basis of bilateral and multilateral relations among states.
Tarique also reaffirmed Bangladesh’s commitment to general and complete disarmament, prevention of the proliferation of nuclear weapons and arms control.
He said Bangladesh would continue to support UN initiatives aimed at promoting global peace and humanity.
On the issue of Palestine, which featured as one of the earliest items in his speech, the Prime Minister said Bangladesh remained unwavering in its support for the legitimate demands of the Palestinian people, including their right to self-determination and to establish an independent State of Palestine.
The Prime Minister said Bangladesh had been sheltering more than 1.2 million forcibly displaced Rohingyas from Myanmar for more than nine years, putting immense pressure on the country’s resources, environment, security and local communities.
He said the source of the Rohingya crisis lay in Myanmar and, therefore, its solution also lay there.
“The only solution to this problem is the safe return of the displaced Rohingya population to their homeland, Myanmar,” he said.
Tarique called for firm and effective support from the UN and the international community for a lasting solution to the crisis.
He also urged the continuation of life-saving humanitarian assistance for the Rohingyas until their repatriation, warning that failure to ensure justice for them could turn the situation into a humanitarian crisis in the near future.
Highlighting Bangladesh’s vulnerability to climate change despite its limited contribution to global carbon emissions, the Prime Minister called for stronger global action at COP31 on climate justice, climate finance and adaptation support.
He said Bangladesh had launched a programme to plant 250 million trees across the country over the next five years and was emphasising clean and solar energy.
The PM also announced a programme to excavate 20,000 kilometres of canals across the country to help protect Bangladesh from floods and droughts.
The government, he said, had also begun implementing the Teesta Master Plan and the Padma Barrage project to increase freshwater flow to the Sundarbans and conserve water through large reservoirs.
He said Bangladesh had reaffirmed its commitment to transboundary water cooperation by signing the 1992 Water Convention.
Tarique said science and technology would shape the future, with artificial intelligence, biotechnology and other scientific advances creating new opportunities.
But he warned against allowing today’s digital divide to become tomorrow’s “artificial intelligence divide.”
He called for technology transfer, skills development and affordable access to modern technologies for developing countries.
“No country should be left behind in this advancement of science,” he said, calling on the UN to adopt an effective policy framework to ensure the positive use of artificial intelligence and social media.
The Prime Minister said Bangladesh remained committed to ensuring regular, safe and orderly migration and called for stronger global cooperation to protect the rights, dignity and welfare of migrants.
As Bangladesh prepares to graduate from the UN’s Least Developed Countries category, he sought continued international support in financing, market access, technology transfer and capacity building to make the transition sustainable.
He also stressed the importance of trade facilitation, connectivity and regional cooperation, saying countries could help one another achieve prosperity through greater economic integration.
As he outlined his vision for Bangladesh, the Prime Minister said "a state can never become strong by keeping its citizens powerless."
He said Bangladesh wanted to establish a prosperous, self-reliant, welfare-oriented democratic state where people regardless of political affiliation, religion or race, could live safely with equal rights, respect and dignity.
“Bangladesh First: Bangladesh for All,” he said, outlining the government’s vision of a country where young people could pursue their dreams without fear, women could live with confidence and every child could realise their full potential.
The Prime Minister concluded by reaffirming Bangladesh’s unwavering support for the principles and values of the United Nations in the cause of world peace.
He addressed the 81st session of the UN General Assembly amid warm applause from delegates present at the UNGA Hall inside UN Headquarters in New York.
He took the podium at around 6:16pm local time to deliver Bangladesh’s national statement at the General Debate.
UNGA President and Bangladesh’s Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman presided over the session, as part of which he introduced the PM and invited him to address the assembly.
Wearing a black suit and red tie, Tarique walked up to the podium and began his address.
It was also a significant moment for the Prime Minister as his late father, President Ziaur Rahman, and mother, former Prime Minister Khaleda Zia, had previously addressed the UN General Assembly from the same podium.
